data.title: The Covenant and Torah
data.sourcePassage: Judaism is one of the world's oldest religions, rooted in the belief in one God and a special covenant between God and the Jewish people. The covenant began with Abraham, when God promised to make his descendants a great nation. It was renewed through Moses at Mount Sinai, where God gave the Torah — the Five Books of Moses — as the guide for Jewish life. The Torah is the most sacred part of Jewish scripture, followed by the Tanakh (the complete Hebrew Bible) and the Talmud (rabbinic interpretations and discussions). Jewish life is shaped by mitzvot — the 613 commandments of the Torah — covering worship, diet, ethics, family, and community. The Shema, from Deuteronomy 6:4, declares: 'Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One.' It is the central Jewish declaration of faith, recited morning and night.

data.title: Shabbat and the Synagogue
data.sourcePassage: Shabbat is the Jewish Sabbath — a weekly day of rest observed from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall. It is the fourth of the Ten Commandments: 'Remember the Sabbath and keep it holy.' Shabbat begins when the mother traditionally lights two candles and says a blessing. The family then says Kiddush over wine and shares challah bread before the Friday evening synagogue service. On Saturday morning there is another synagogue service including the reading of a passage from the Torah scroll. Shabbat ends with the Havdalah ceremony, using a twisted candle, wine, and sweet-smelling spices. The synagogue is the Jewish place of community and worship. It contains the Aron HaKodesh (Holy Ark) which holds the Torah scrolls, the Ner Tamid (Eternal Light) above the Ark, and the Bimah — the raised platform from which the Torah is read.

data.title: Pesach and Yom Kippur
data.sourcePassage: Pesach — also called Passover — is the most widely observed Jewish festival. It commemorates the liberation of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, as told in the book of Exodus. The centrepiece of Pesach is the Seder meal, at which the family retells the Exodus story using food, song, and scripture from a special book called the Haggadah. The youngest child asks 'Why is tonight different from all other nights?' and the story is told in reply. Bitter herbs represent the bitterness of slavery; matzah (unleavened bread) recalls the haste of departure from Egypt. Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, is the holiest day of the Jewish year. Jews fast for 25 hours, attend synagogue throughout the day, and confess sins and seek forgiveness from God and those they have wronged. It is a solemn day focused on honesty, repentance, and repair of relationships.
